science.title: A nearly 100-million-year-old hairy snail pays tribute to the Prodigy's lead singer
science.description: Myanmar amber (more commonly known as "burmite") is one of the most important sources of information about biodiversity during the Mesozoic Era. This amber dates back to the age of the dinosaurs and is approximately 99 million years old. Burmite preserves numerous now-extinct organisms (animals, plants, fungi, etc.) as inclusions, often in astonishing detail. This is because amber can preserve even soft tissues, which would otherwise decompose rapidly, and do so in three dimensions.

science.title: Nonlinear frequency scaling and amplitude correction for cost-efficient parameter tuning of passive microwave components
science.description: Numerical optimization driven by full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulations plays a central role in the design of microwave circuits. It is used to improve system performance and to compensate for inaccuracies in simpler representations, analytical or equivalent network models, routinely employed at the beginning of the design process. A persistent issue is the high cost of simulation-driven parameter tuning, which often requires hundreds of system simulations. Reducing this cost without compromising reliability is imperative to shortening design cycles in both academia and industry. This article introduces a novel approach to cost-efficient design closure of microwave components. The keystones of our methodology are the employment of an auxiliary low-fidelity EM model and its correction, launched as soon as the search process starts converging. Model enhancement is achieved through a nonlinear mapping of the evaluation frequency, implemented using splines and anchor points distributed across the spectrum of interest, as well as multiplicative amplitude scaling. The aforementioned scheme enforces zero-order agreement between the fine EM model and low-fidelity one, as well as renders an accurate representation of the circuit responses near the current iteration point (at which the correction has been established). The computational benefits come from performing most EM analyses at low resolution. As demonstrated using three microstrip circuits, the savings with regard to the baseline algorithm reach seventy percent on average. The presented method is also shown to be faster than a number of accelerated benchmark algorithms, with the speedup achieved with only a minor loss in design quality.
